opus-5.5.text:
I think the thing I like most is that you can have a conversation with it. When you read a proof in a paper, it's static: the author made choices about what to spell out and what to skip, and if you get stuck on a step, you're kind of on your own. With a model, you can just stop and ask, "Why does this inequality hold?" or "What's the intuition behind choosing this particular construction?" and it'll unpack it for you at whatever level you need.

It's also really good for the zoomed-out view. Sometimes I'll ask it to sketch the overall structure first: what are the two or three key ideas, and where is the hard part? Then I can dive into the details knowing where I'm headed. That's usually how a good human mentor would explain something, and it's nice to have that available anytime.

And I like that I can push back. If I think a step is wrong, I can say so, and either it convinces me or we find that there's actually a gap. That back-and-forth is a big part of how you really understand mathematics, rather than just nodding along. Of course, you still have to check things yourself, since models can make mistakes, but as a thinking partner for working through a proof, it's been genuinely useful.

r001.rationale: The candidate says you can pause while reading a proof and ask the model questions about a step or construction to understand it.

fable-5.1.text:
What I like most is that it changes the kind of attention I can give a proof. Normally when I read a proof, a lot of my effort goes into bookkeeping: tracking what each symbol means, checking that a bound really holds, figuring out which lemma a step is quietly invoking. That work matters, but it isn't where the understanding lives. With a model, I can hand off a lot of that. I can ask, "Why is this inequality tight here?" or "What breaks if we drop this hypothesis?" and get a fast, concrete answer instead of spending twenty minutes reconstructing it myself.

The other thing is that it's patient in a way a textbook or a paper can't be. A paper is written once, for one imagined reader. A model can re-explain the same step at three different levels, or translate an argument into the language I already know. If I'm reading something in a field I'm not fluent in, I can ask it to recast the proof in terms of an analogy I understand, and then ask where the analogy fails. That failure point is usually exactly the idea the proof is really about.

And I'd say it makes me a more active reader. When I read alone, it's easy to nod along and think I've understood something I haven't. When I'm in a conversation, I'm constantly generating questions, and the model's answers expose where my mental model was vague. Sometimes the model is wrong, and catching that is also useful, because it forces me to articulate precisely why a step does or doesn't work. The goal isn't to have the model understand the proof for me. It's to get to the point where I can explain it myself, and the back-and-forth gets me there faster.

r001.rationale: It describes asking the model follow-up questions about proof steps and assumptions to deepen understanding of how the proof works.

astra-6.text:
What I like is that you can ask questions at exactly the level where you’re stuck. When you read a proof, there might be a step that the author considers obvious, but you don’t see why it follows. You can ask the model to unpack that step, work through a small example, or explain what a particular assumption is doing.

And you can keep asking follow-up questions without feeling like you’re slowing anyone down. You still have to check the reasoning—the model can make mistakes—but that back-and-forth can help you get from being able to follow a proof to understanding why it works.

r001.rationale: It describes asking the model follow-up questions about proof steps and assumptions as a way to move from following a proof to understanding why it works.
